text: In SQL Server, every table uses the same storage mechanism underneath — there's no choice to make, and transactions, foreign keys, and row-level locking are always just available. MySQL is built differently. It supports multiple, swappable storage engines, chosen per table, and that choice genuinely changes which SQL features actually work against that table.

InnoDB is MySQL's modern default, and what almost everyone should be using. Create table orders, with a foreign key back to customers, engine equals InnoDB. Transactions, foreign key enforcement, row-level locking for concurrent access — everything you've always assumed just exists in T-SQL.

MyISAM is older, and genuinely missing things you'd assume every database table has. No transaction support at all. No foreign key enforcement. And it locks at the TABLE level, not the row level, so one writer blocks every other reader and writer on that entire table.

Here's why this is a real developer problem, not just a DBA curiosity. Start transaction, update accounts, update a MyISAM table, then ROLLBACK. The accounts update rolls back fine — it's InnoDB. The MyISAM update never rolls back, because MyISAM was never part of the transaction to begin with. Your error-handling code runs, reports success, and the database is left half-updated, silently.
Before you write transactional code against any table, check its engine. SHOW TABLE STATUS where name equals the table, or SHOW CREATE TABLE, both reveal the engine directly, in seconds.

InnoDB for transactions, foreign keys, and row-level locking. MyISAM for none of those, silently. Always check before you trust ROLLBACK. Next lesson, we put this whole chapter together: translating one complete, real T-SQL query into correct MySQL, line by line. See you there.
